newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Mentor Ophthalmics' IOL.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Mentor Ophthalmics' IOL.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory committee voted 11-0 on Thursday to approve a new intraocular lens (IOL) made by Mentor Corp's Mentor Ophthalmics.

The MemoryLens, recommended for people over age 60, is approved in 50 countries. It is smaller than conventional IOL's, and arrives in the operating room pre-rolled, making it easier to insert, reducing operating time and complications.
IOL's, which have global sales of about $400 million, are used to replace normal lenses damaged by cataracts. Foldable lenses are expected to begin capturing more of the market.
Panelists concluded that MemoryLens is effective. Main studies were of an earlier, flat version of MemoryLens, collected by its developer Optical Radiation.

A year after implantation, 97 percent of patients recovered vision of 20-40 or better, noted panelist Eve Higginbotham of the University of Maryland School of Medicine. She said MemoryLens "appears to be very safe."
There were complications, however. In the main studies, 3.9 percent of patients had hyphema, or bleeding into the chamber of the eye, compared with an expected one percent.

Higginbotham said the hyphema was probably due to insertion problems, as it was not seen in a 190-patient study of the pre-rolled MemoryLens also considered by the panel. The glaucoma rate was high with just over four percent of patients having increased intraocular pressure shortly after surgery.

Committee member Kevin Greenidge of the State University of New York Health Science Center said that he thought this was a "safety issue." Mentor claimed that the glaucoma was "transient", and dissipated with time. Greenidge said that his concerns had been satisfied by Mentor.

The panel also discussed a high incidence of "haze" that occurred just after surgery in patients in the pre-rolled lens study. Higginbotham said she doubted that "there's any causal relationship associated with the lens."

There will be a growing need for IOLs as the population ages. But due to declining reimbursement, IOL sales will drop from $270 million in the U.S. in 1995 to $208 million by 2000, projects Theta Research of Rocky Hill, Conn.

Medicare spends $2 billion a year for lenses and surgery fees but has been reducing the amount it pays per lens. It now pays about $150 per lens, down from $200 several years ago. Managed care organizations have followed suit, says Theta.
